lesson.title: The Alphabet & buchstabieren
lesson.subtitle: W = 'veh', V = 'fow', J = 'yot', Z = 'tsett', ß = 'Eszett' — spell it like a native

hook.title: The Letter Names the Shifts Explain
hook.content: German letter names are tiny history lessons. W is 'veh' and V is 'fow' — because German V is pronounced [f], the very fact the V→B family is built on. J is 'yot' — the y-sound English split away in the y→g family. Z is 'tsett' — the /ts/ affricate of the T→Z shift, said aloud as a letter name. And ß is 'Eszett' — literally 's-z', the sharp s of Straße. Now the verb for using them: buchstabieren, 'to spell', built on Buchstabe 'letter' — literally a book-staff, the beech-wood stick once used to mark reading passages — plus the -ieren suffix you already own from the Latin Bridge. A native root wearing a Latin suit.

footnotes.title: Buchstabe's Wooden Secret
footnotes.content: Buchstabe comes from Old High German buohstabe: buoh (book) + stab (staff, stick — the same word as English stave). Before printing, runes and reading pointers were carved beechwood sticks — Buche is beech — so a 'letter' was literally a book-stave. English kept the wooden cousin in 'stave' and 'staff'.

pattern.title: Spelling Aloud, the German Way
pattern.content: The trap letters: W = veh (English V's sound), V = fow (English F's sound), J = yot (English Y's sound), Z = tsett (English TS), ß = Eszett (sharp S). In speech, German sp- and st- at the start of a word sound like 'shp-' and 'sht-', and Sch- is always 'sh': sprechen, Stein, schreiben. On the phone, Germans spell with the formula: 'Wie schreibt man das? — Buchstabieren Sie bitte: B wie Berta, E wie Emil...' The verb is regular except for the stress: buchstabieren, ich buchstabiere, past participle buchstabiert — and remember the Latin Bridge rule: no ge- on -ieren verbs.
pattern.linguist_note: Letter names fossilize pronunciation history: German kept the continental Romance values (V = [f] before it shifted, J = [j]) while English drifted to its own. When you say 'fow' for V, you are pronouncing the medieval consonant system out loud — the same one that makes Vater a [f]-word.

exercises.prompt: Match each German letter with its name:
exercises.explanation: V = fow because German V sounds like [f] — the letter name is the V→B family's origin story said out loud.

exercises.prompt: How is the letter V pronounced in German words like 'Vater'?
exercises.meaning: German V = [f] — hence Vater's [f] and the letter name 'fow'
exercises.explanation: German V is the [f] of Vater/Vogel/Vier — which is exactly why Vater is a Verner's-law twin of father, not a V→B word.

exercises.meaning: to spell = letter + the Latin-style -ieren suffix
exercises.explanation: A Germanic root in a Latin suit: Buchstabe is native (book-staff), -ieren is the productive loan-suffix from the Latin Bridge.
No English cognate here — 'spell' is a different word. Buchstabieren must be memorized, but its Buchstabe core makes it transparent.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the German sentence you hear:
exercises.meaning: Kannst du das bitte buchstabieren = can you spell that please

vocab_hints.note: spelled on the phone as Ö wie Öl — Germans use a familiar word when a letter is hard to name
T wie Theodor, Ü wie Übermut, T wie Theodor, E wie Emil — the chain that spells the bag you are holding
sich ausziehen — reflexive, with the aus- 'out' prefix from topic 15 — and it hides a Z, the tsett-letter from exercise one

exercises.explanation: Modal kannst in position 2, the -ieren infinitive at the bracket's end — and no ge- ever touches its participle.
cues: Meaning: "Kannst du das bitte buchstabieren = can you spell that please"
Opens with "Kannst du" and ends with "buchstabieren".

summary.outcome: Recite the trap letter names (veh, fow, yot, tsett, Eszett) and spell your name with buchstabieren.

use_example.german: Wie schreibt man das? Kannst du das bitte buchstabieren?
use_example.english: How do you write that? Can you spell it please?

summary.takeaway: The letter names are the shifts made audible: W=veh, V=fow, J=yot, Z=tsett, ß=Eszett — and buchstabieren is Buchstabe + -ieren.

buchstabieren.etymology_derivation: Buchstabe (letter, 'book-staff') + -ieren — a native root with the Latin-style -ieren verb suffix. [wiktionary]

buch.context_translation: I am reading a good book.

schreiben.etymology_derivation: A Latin loan (scribere) that both languages Germanicized — English kept it in scribe, script, describe. Strong verb: schrieb, geschrieben. [wiktionary]

wort.etymology_derivation: Final d → t. Plural: Wörter / Worte.

buchstabe.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *bōkstabô, literally book-stave: each letter was a stave carved for writing, first on beechwood; the page compares English bookstaff and bookstave. [wiktionary]

öl.context_phrase: Ich brate das Ei in Öl.
öl.context_translation: I fry the egg in oil.
öl.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic oli, meaning olive oil, ultimately from Latin oleum; English oil descends from the same early Latin loan into Old English. [wiktionary]

tüte.etymology_derivation: From Low German tute, a conical bag — the page lists English tote as the cognate: the bag you tote things in. [wiktionary]

ausziehen.english_cognate: to take off, to move out
ausziehen.english_meaning: to take off, to move out
ausziehen.context_phrase: Zuhause ziehe ich die Schuhe aus.
ausziehen.context_translation: At home I take off my shoes.
ausziehen.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + ziehen (to pull): aus is the t-to-s twin of English out, and the root is the *teuhaną of English tug. [wiktionary]

boden.context_translation: The floor is made of wood.
boden.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *budm-, variant of *butmaz — explicitly cognate with English bottom. [wiktionary]

mehl.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic melu; English meal, in its older sense of ground grain, is a direct cognate. [wiktionary]

wunderbar.etymology_derivation: Wunder 'wonder' + -bar '-able' — literally wonder-able; Wunder is the twin of English wonder (Proto-Germanic *wundran, per etymonline). [wiktionary] [etymonline]

augenbraue.etymology_derivation: A compound of Auge and Braue, from Middle High German ougenbrāwe. English brow is the cognate of Braue. [wiktionary]

notfall.context_phrase: Im Notfall drücken Sie die Taste.
notfall.context_translation: In an emergency press the button.
notfall.etymology_derivation: Not (need, distress — twin of English need) plus Fall (case, fall — twin of English fall); literally need-fall, an emergency. [wiktionary]

landkarte.context_phrase: Wir suchen den Weg auf der Landkarte.
landkarte.context_translation: We look for the way on the map.
landkarte.etymology_derivation: Land + Karte, both documented twins: land, and Karte the twin of card (both from Latin charta) — a land-card, that is, a map. [wiktionary]

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs NEVER take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert, reparieren → repariert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Adopted from Old French -ier in Middle High German as the universal productive suffix for foreign loan verbs.
